scope: Independent tone review of exactly the 11 toddler-limits r02 entries and their 18–24-month placements, including every assigned frozen topic row and detail render. All 11 openingText values and art contexts are null. Source/context reading is evidence, not a publication or release approval.

inputIdentity.checks: Recomputed selected snapshot-file hashes and checked them against MANIFEST; checked component-hash strings and null art against each snapshot; verified assigned authored entries equal frozen entries and payload entries, and assigned provenance references/public age qualifications match their frozen public fields. Source identity matched the original PDF. No claims of review from a research-ready flag or author read log.

independence: I did not author these entries or read another reviewer’s reports. Read only assigned companion bodies/provenance and placements. The sole wider companion scan was titles in the 18–24-month Connection & feelings topic, to judge recognizability and repetition. No unassigned entry bodies/provenance were used.

surfaceRead.description: Personally read each assigned RENDERED_SURFACES topicRows.text/topicRows.html and complete entryText, the exact snapshot public projection and src/HomeStudy.jsx. The renderer shows each summary in its topic row and again in detail, and exposes reference locators verbatim. No browser screenshot/layout review is claimed. The title-only topic scan did not justify a blanket rewrite of ordinary “room” or “small part” expressions.

textPlacement.assessment: The topic summaries retain “when you can,” and the detail makes finishing recognizable through one last turn or saving work. It preserves unwanted-choice variation and gentle adult help when it is time to leave, without a timer rule, clock-understanding expectation or promised agreement. Both Everyday care and Connection & feelings are appropriate retrieval contexts.

The short row already pairs time with showing what the adult means; nonresponse is not labeled defiance or diagnosed as processing. The detail adds respectful necessary-transition language and ordinary humor without a response deadline or guaranteed result. This is a useful natural suggestion in both assigned topics; “room for processing” does not require a blanket style rewrite.

issues.surface: connection-feelings topic title and detail body
issues.finding: “Let them help think of a way” does not identify the situation. The body stays with “part of a solution,” “a plan you can both live with,” and “a concern” without giving one actual problem or child contribution. The source’s PDF 119 examples make the idea much easier to picture, especially its preverbal child offering a sibling another toy. The current prose is respectful but leaves a parent with an abstract process.
issues.requiredCorrection: Make the title identify an ordinary disagreement or recurring problem, and add one concise, source-supported example of a toddler’s contribution from PDF 119. Preserve the adult’s leadership, the possibility that the adult supplies most ideas, preverbal participation, revision of an unhelpful plan and the immediate-protection exception. No formal meeting or required child solution is needed.

textPlacement.assessment: Adult leadership, preverbal participation, most ideas coming from the adult, revisiting the plan and the limits of notes are all preserved. The remaining tone/usefulness problem is identifiable and narrow: the title and explanation need a recognizable problem and one concrete example, as recorded in TL-TONE-004.

The row identifies waiting rooms and cafés, and the detail offers books, watching airport activity and a walk together. The text acknowledges that an adult may need to change expectations during a visit without calling restlessness bad behavior or guaranteeing cooperation. It avoids turning the source’s small-object travel examples into a shopping list or material recommendation.

The row keeps safety, respectful life and the child’s disappointment together. The detail gives one related response with a later retry, permits thoughtful revision and acknowledgment of a changed mind, and treats the checklist as Davies’s questions rather than a parent scorecard. It preserves adult limits without requiring a pleased or compliant child.

issues.surface: connection-feelings topic row and repeated detail-page summary
issues.finding: “Explanation and repair come after calm” makes repair sound like the routine next step after a tantrum. This entry’s cue includes disappointment or frustration without any harm. Davies says to help make amends if needed (PDF 135) and distinguishes accepting feelings from addressing damage or harm (PDF 137–139). The unqualified short sentence risks making the feeling itself something the child must put right.
issues.requiredCorrection: Keep calm before discussion, and explicitly condition making amends on something needing repair, such as harm or damage. Put that condition in the summary itself; do not rely on another entry or a detail-only clarification. Preserve the existing comfort, declined-touch, protection and necessary-departure qualifications.

issues.surface: detail page / Back to the books
issues.finding: The renderer exposes “Complete support, declined touch, public/time qualifications, recap triggers and calm-before-repair” verbatim. “Public/time qualifications” and “recap triggers” read as internal editorial coverage notes, rather than a useful locator for a parent returning to the book.
issues.requiredCorrection: Replace this locator with ordinary reader-facing subjects, for example comfort during tantrums, declined touch, tantrums in public or when leaving, and making amends when needed. Keep the precise source pages and any editorial coverage notes in provenance.

textPlacement.assessment: Comfort is offered, declined touch is respected, protection remains immediate, and the detail preserves public-space and necessary-departure conditions. Trigger descriptions are tentative and carry no prevention guarantee. TL-TONE-001 is required because the summary still makes repair sound universal; TL-TONE-002 is limited to the visible reference locator.

This repair entry identifies hurt people, damaged belongings or a mess in its context and supplies concrete ways to join an adult: checking on a person, bringing a tissue or gathering thrown things. Calm comes first, adult help is explicit, apology is modeled rather than required, and the child’s experience remains part of the conversation. It does not require a young toddler to repair alone or promise an immediate change in feeling.

The short row places stopping hitting/biting/pushing alongside understanding and keeps repair after calm. Detail maintains protection before later observation, uses concrete situational clues, and does not turn laughter into proof of motive. It avoids diagnostic, nervous-system, injury-treatment and guaranteed-phase-ending claims. The guidance remains descriptive of Davies’s approach.

issues.finding: “The underlying question is which movement the child is seeking” assumes that a particular sought movement explains the objects being pushed or thrown. The cited passage asks the adult to look for patterns and offers throwing opportunities; it does not establish the motive of this child in this incident. The otherwise careful entry shifts from attributed possibilities into an unqualified interpretation.
issues.requiredCorrection: Describe Davies’s offered movement outlet or phrase it as a possibility to consider while observing, without asserting what the child is seeking. Retain protection of people/belongings, possible removal of wooden objects and clear limits. This needs a sentence-level correction, not removal of the throwing topic.

textPlacement.assessment: Both assigned topic rows carry pattern noticing and protection, and the body retains the wooden-object caution and indoor/outdoor distinction. The title makes throwing recognizable. TL-TONE-003 addresses only the final sentence’s assumption about the child’s sought movement; an appropriate throwing outlet can remain as Davies’s suggestion.

The title and cue make the situation recognizable without labeling the child clingy. Possible reasons remain possibilities; shared play and laundry give ordinary examples; supervision and the absence of an hours-long solo-play expectation are explicit. Announced departures are not expanded into separation training. The modest “small part” language is tied to actual shared work, not a performance requirement.

The short row establishes ordinary conversation, acknowledgment and returning at a pause. The detail retains the adult’s prompt listening, practice without a waiting-duration target, and the urgent-help boundary. It presents one source example rather than a rule that a child must perform the signal to earn attention.

learnings.observation: The r02 tantrum summary loses the source’s conditional repair language even though its comfort, safety and time qualifications are retained; the separate repair entry cannot supply that condition to a reader scanning the tantrum row.
learnings.action: For this companion’s tantrum surfaces, keep the harm/damage condition beside any statement about making amends, including the topic summary.

learnings.observation: HomeStudy renders reference.locator as parent-facing prose; the r02 tantrum locator includes internal coverage shorthand such as public/time qualifications.
learnings.action: Write locators as recognizable book subjects and preserve coverage shorthand only in private provenance.
